## Problem

`\u202c` (and similar Unicode characters) can't be encoded in latin-1. The fix is to strip them from all string columns before the export call, leaving everything else untouched.

---

## Fix

```python
# Strip characters that latin-1 can't encode from all string columns
Historial = Historial.apply(
    lambda col: col.map(
        lambda x: x.encode('latin-1', errors='ignore').decode('latin-1')
        if isinstance(x, str) else x
    )
    if col.dtype == object else col
)

Historial.to_csv("C:/Users/80732688/Downloads/Demográficos/Historial_formularios_consolidado_latin1.csv",index=False,sep=";",decimal=",",encoding='latin-1')
```

---

## How it works

| Step | What happens |
|---|---|
| `col.dtype == object` | Targets only string/object columns, leaves numerics alone |
| `.encode('latin-1', errors='ignore')` | Drops any character that has no latin-1 representation (like `\u202c`) |
| `.decode('latin-1')` | Converts the cleaned bytes back to a plain string |
| Everything else | `sep`, `decimal`, `index`, path, and encoding stay exactly as they were |

---

## Note

`errors='ignore'` **silently drops** unencodable characters. If you'd rather replace them with a placeholder (e.g. `?`), swap it for `errors='replace'` in the encode call.

## Characters this removes

`\u202c` is the **Pop Directional Formatting** mark — an invisible Unicode control character with no latin-1 equivalent. `errors='ignore'` silently drops it and anything else outside the latin-1 range (`0x00–0xFF`).
